Seven close friends in China decided to build their dream home so they could retire and live together. They found a spot in the countryside near Guangzhou and spent around 4 million yuan (about $580,000 USD) to construct a spacious and peaceful mansion surrounded by nature. The house has large glass windows, open common areas, individual bedrooms for each of them, and a shared kitchen. They even included a tea pavilion where they can gather, drink tea, and enjoy each other's company. The idea came from a casual conversation, but they made it real by combining their savings and working closely with designers. They also made a plan for the future: they'll take care of one another as they grow older and even hire a cook and caretaker if needed. Their dream was to grow old together not in isolation, but with laughter, support, and lifelong friendship. #fyp #blowup #friends #story

desc: “Anti-Chinese sentiment is a fear or dislike of China, Chinese people or Chinese culture, also referred to as Sinophobia.” I can go on and on about how beautiful traditional Chinese culture is, study years and years and never know the entire history of my ancestor’s country, practice hours and hours and still not be able to master my guzheng… but all of this work, it seems reduced to nothing at the face of sinophobia. Why is it that our traditional culture is belittled because of modern politics? Why is it that, when popular trends which are appreciated by all, suddenly become controversial when the public finds out its origin is in China? ‘K-beauty’ ‘Korean nails’ ‘Japanese makeup’, at what point do we have to realise many of those products and trends are Chinese? Or perhaps we should just be happy that it is appreciated for what it is, and not discriminated against because the public doesn’t know of its origins?  I am an ABC. I am a proud Australian. But I am also of Chinese descent. I love my ancestor’s culture and I will always defend its beauty against biased people and introduce its wonders to people who are appreciative of differences. Love your culture, and encourage others to love it too. desc: Chinese breakfast is wild #china #chinesefood #chinalife #chinese #chinatravel

In 2007, China labeled unmarried women over 27 “leftover.” By 2024, marriages had crashed fifty-five percent from their peak. And they can’t undo it. The setup: China has 30 million more men than women of marriage age. In the manufacturing city of Dongguan, the ratio runs 139 men for every 100 women. There's an arithmetic bride shortage the one-child policy created. So the women who did exist, with the degrees the state spent decades encouraging them to earn, should have been in demand. Instead, the Ministry of Education put a word in the dictionary.  Sheng nu. Leftover women. Same character as leftover food. The All-China Women's Federation spread it through state media, calling educated single women “already old, like yellowed pearls.” The word did something specific. In the 2016 SK-II documentary filmed at Shanghai's People's Park marriage market, a mother explains on camera, with her daughter sitting right there, that the daughter is “average looking, not too pretty,” and that's why she's leftover. The daughter holds her composure for about three seconds. Sociologist Leta Hong Fincher documented women using the state's own vocabulary to describe their terror of the label. Even the pushback kept the word alive. SK-II's campaign got 44 million views and nearly doubled their China sales. But to argue leftover women weren't actually leftover, they had to keep saying “leftover women.” The self-declared leftover social clubs in Shanghai and Beijing, the Western journalists, the fashion editors: everyone was arguing inside vocabulary the state had installed. Now China recorded just 6.1 million marriages in 2024. The fertility rate is 1.09. And in February 2026, the government ordered platforms to censor marriage skepticism. The state wrote the word into the dictionary in an afternoon. It has no clear mechanism for writing it back out.

Chinese culture is one of the oldest cultures in the world, with a history of over 5,000 years. It is known for its strong traditions, respect for family, and important contributions to art, science, and technology. Family is very important in Chinese culture. People are taught to respect their parents and elders, and families often celebrate holidays together. Education is also highly valued, and students are encouraged to work hard and succeed. The main language is Mandarin Chinese, and the writing system uses thousands of characters. Chinese food is famous worldwide, with popular dishes such as noodles, dumplings, and rice. Different regions have their own unique cooking styles. Chinese New Year is the country’s biggest holiday and is celebrated with family gatherings, fireworks, dragon dances, and red envelopes. Other traditions include the Mid-Autumn Festival and the Dragon Boat Festival. China is also known for famous landmarks like the Great Wall and for inventions such as paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass. Today, China combines ancient traditions with modern technology, making its culture one of the most influential in the world. #fyp #chinese #viral #humor #funny

desc: Which one do you prefer? China can look completely different during the day versus the night, and both are stunning in its own way! During our recent trip to China, we explored ancient towns and mountains during the day, and experience the vibrant city life at night. If you are thinking about a trip to China, save this guide and follow for more China travel inspo!  🌃 CHONGQING 🟢 Hongyadong 洪崖洞 is best visited around sunset so you can see it before and after the lights turn on.  🟢 Liziba Station 李子坝站 is where Chongqing’s Line 2 monorail appears to travel directly through a building.  🟢 Luohan Temple 罗汉寺 is a peaceful Buddhist temple surrounded by Chongqing’s skyscrapers. 🐼 CHENGDU 🟢 Visit the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding early in the morning when pandas tend to be more active. 🟢 Head to Chunxi Road and Taikoo Li after dark for shopping, food and the giant 3D panda screen. 🟢 Tower of Life is especially impressive after dark when the structure is illuminated. ⛰️ ZHANGJIAJIE 🟢 Allow at least 2 - 3 days for Zhangjiajie National Forest Park. Highlights include Yuanjiajie, Tianzi Mountain and the Bailong Elevator. 🟢 Stay near Wulingyuan for easier access to the national park. 🟢 Add Tianmen Mountain if you have another day. It is a separate attraction closer to Zhangjiajie city. 🏮 FURONG TOWN 🟢 This ancient town is built directly around a waterfall and is best experienced after dark when the buildings illuminate. 💧 DUJIANGYAN 🟢 Visit the Dujiangyan Irrigation System, an engineering project dating back more than 2,000 years that still helps control and distribute water today. 🟢 After dark, head into Dujiangyan city to see the famous glowing blue water known online as the Blue Tears. 🌆 GUANGZHOU 🟢 Head to the Canton Tower and the Zhujiang New Town waterfront around sunset. Stay after dark to see the tower and Guangzhou’s modern skyline illuminated along the Pearl River. 🟢 Explore Yongqing Fang 永庆坊 and the surrounding Xiguan area for historic Cantonese architecture alongside restored shops, cafés and restaurants. 🟢 Make time for Dim Sum while you’re here! Guangzhou is one of the best places to experience traditional Cantonese morning tea.

desc: Everywhere I possibly go #livinginchina #foreignerinchina #chinalife #livingabroad

American Factory (2019) is a documentary about Chinese company Fuyao’s takeover of a shuttered General Motors plant in the American Rust Belt of Dayton, Ohio. As Fuyao send their own employees and laborers to work alongside the Americans, cultural differences and tensions emerge. The Chinese, with their high efficiency, strict hierarchies, and group-over-individual mindset, feel like a robotic  threat to American laborers, while ideal for American managers. Individually-minded American workers are more concerned with securing labor rights and unionizing than matching the efficiency of the Chinese. For the billionaire chairman of Fuyao, unionizing poses a threat to his profit, and the Chinese laborers are dissuaded and ultimately unable to see the value of supporting unionization.  Despite not seeing eye-to-eye at work, some Chinese and American workers find personal parallels regarding the hardship of working-class/immigrant life, emotional connection, and friendship. A standout moment was when the American management team traveled to China to observe the highly efficient Fuyao factories and attend the Fuyao employee Chinese New Year banquet. The beauty of Chinese culture moves one American to tears, and he chokes out the film’s main message, “We’re one big planet somewhat divided, but we’re one.” #documentary #chinesefilm #china #uschina #factory #factorywork #laborunion #capitalism #eastmeetswest #americanfactory #netflix #chinesenewyear #fuyao #chinesefactory #workingclass #filmanalysis

desc: After years of living in China, I’ve honestly come to see street food as better than restaurant food most of the time. Of course there are exceptions, but the best street vendors usually have a personal stake in every dish they serve. They’re cooking the same handful of specialties day after day, refining them over years, sometimes decades. There’s a sense of pride and care that’s hard to replicate in a larger restaurant. And beyond the food itself, there’s something deeply satisfying about eating on the street. No fancy décor, no presentation tricks—just great food, fresh air, and everyday life happening around you. It feels more honest, more connected to the place and the people who live there. Restaurants can offer comfort and occasion, but street food often offers something rarer: authenticity. #china #chinesefood #streetfood #familytime #chinalife

desc: One thing about living abroad: your definition of 'normal' completely changes. My heart still skips a beat seeing these scooter rides. Would you trust your balance riding like this? #china #cultureshock #wtf #safety #toddler

growing up in Hong Kong in a very traditional Chinese family, being gay just wasn’t an option. As a kid, I knew deep down that I liked girls. But my family was so conservative, and I loved them. I held out hope that maybe I just hadn’t met the right guy yet. I didn’t want to disappoint everyone.  in college in the US, I realized that was never going to happen. I’m 100% a lesbian🤪 And that’s when I met Madi!  we grew up so differently- her in Houston TX, me in Hong Kong. We were worlds apart. Madi grew up VERY southern and basically lived off a diet of chicken tenders and Mac & cheese. So it was extra meaningful that she was always trying to learn more about where I came from. At dim sum, she would be down to try everything🥺🥺 she even went out of her way to look up the dates and meanings of Chinese holidays. One day, I came over to her apartment on Chinese new year (I had totally forgotten it had started) and she had set up some flowers for me and even written a note in Chinese inside a red packet😭😭 (I told her afterwards that u don’t rly give red packets to your peers but it’s the thought that counts) I’ll never forget when she brought me to the rodeo in Houston and I met her family. Even though they were catholic and were nervous about meeting me, they welcomed me with open arms. Now, they invite me over for every family occasion. Madi’s mom even made me my own personalized stocking for Christmas 🥹  Finally, I decided to take madi home to meet my family in Hong Kong. I had never brought anyone home before😳 But before long, I realized I had nothing to be nervous about. My dad (as a typical Chinese man does) tried to outdrink madi at dinner, but his lightweight ass could NOT compete. He was automatically impressed by her 😏 Madi played arcade games with my brother and went kayaking with my sister. She vibed with everyone🥹 Now, we’ve been married for over a year and a half, and it’s been the best year of my life. Our home truly combines the best parts of how we grew up. We see her family every Christmas, and see my family in Hong Kong every summer. Shoutout to summer break for teachers🤪🤪 We celebrate Chinese holidays like mid-autumn festival, and I sometimes go to mass with her at our local church (shoutout to Catholic Lesbians group at St Francis Xavier in NYC🏳️‍🌈🏳️‍🌈🏳️‍🌈)! Our diet is a mix of collard greens, stir-fried Chinese vegetables, seafood boils, and congee.  If only little me could see our life together. I know she would be proud🥰

Rongjiang County has just been lifted out of poverty and is a small county town on the 18th line. Rongjiang has a mild climate and abundant rainfall. mountain area. In the past few days, Rongjiang County in Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, Guizhou Province, which has been hit by the nationwide outbreak of "village floods", has suffered a once-in-a-decade catastrophic flood disaster. The officers and soldiers of the stationed troops in Guizhou, as well as the militia, rushed to the scene to carry out rescue operations upon hearing the order. The Rongjiang County Fire and Rescue Brigade participated in the rescue overnight, actively transferring and evacuating the distressed people through boats, ropes and other equipment in the main streets of the county At 17:00 on June 28, the Guizhou Meteorological Station announced that the heavy rainfall had weakened significantly, and the blue warning of rainstorm was lifted. It is expected that the rainfall in the Duliujiang River Basin will significantly decrease in the future, but secondary disasters still need to be prevented. ------------- Rongjiang County is under the jurisdiction of Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture in Guizhou Province. Located in the southeastern part of Guizhou Province, in the southern part of Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture. It borders Liping County and Congjiang County to the east, Leishan County and Sandu Shui Autonomous County to the west, Jianhe County to the north, and Libo County to the south, with a total area of 3316 square kilometers and a total population of 385000. It is a multi-ethnic mixed population county, with ethnic minorities accounting for 81% of the total population and a total of 16 ethnic groups. #Guizhou#Rongjiang#flood #cn #top #china #hot #pla #soldier

desc: China never fails to amaze me. 🇨🇳✨ Every time I think I’ve seen it all, it surprises me with something completely unexpected. This time, I discovered a place that feels like it came straight out of a sci-fi movie—a retro cyberpunk-style food hall hidden in the heart of Changsha. Imagine neon lights glowing from every corner, vintage storefronts blending seamlessly with futuristic design, creating a space that feels like stepping into a cyberpunk dream. ⚡🍜💫 But the most unbelievable part? A real cable car slowly glides right through the food hall. 🚡🤯 Yes, an actual cable car passes overhead while people are enjoying their meals, making it feel as if you’re dining in another dimension where the past and the future exist together. What surprised me even more is that hardly anyone seems to talk about this place online. It’s such an underrated hidden gem, full of creativity, atmosphere, and incredible attention to detail. Every corner has its own story, and every glowing light feels carefully designed to transport you somewhere else. And the food? Absolutely incredible. I tried the crayfish 🦞—rich, spicy, packed with flavor, and honestly the best I’ve ever had. I couldn’t stop eating! 🔥 If you’re ever visiting Changsha, don’t miss this place. It’s much more than a restaurant—it’s an unforgettable journey through time, imagination, and some of the best food you’ll find in the city. 🌃💖 📍Wenheyou (文和友) 36 Xiangjiang Middle Road, Tianxin District, Changsha, China #chinatravel #visitchina #chinathroughmyeyes #rimmasjourney #changsha

desc: Divine Mortise & Tenon: Crafting Traditional Rosewood Furniture #山白 #Shanbai #China｜榫卯天成 ——传统红木家具制作 Divine Mortise & Tenon: The Craft of Rosewood Furniture Traditional Chinese rosewood furniture requires no nails or glue, relying entirely on interlocking mortise and tenon joints. Craftsmen calculate timber angles precisely, carving mortises and tenons to create seamless, stable connections. Joints fit naturally following wood grain, ensuring lasting durability without auxiliary materials. The whole workflow follows ancient techniques: timber selection, cutting, shaping, carving, repeated sanding and fine polishing. More than merely a craft, mortise and tenon embodies ancient wisdom of harmony between humanity and nature, integrating mechanical principles into woodenware. Interlocking components balance rigidity and gentleness. Rosewood furniture combines practical function with oriental aesthetics, inheriting thousands of years of Chinese craftsmanship.  榫卯天成——红木家具的制作。中国传统红木家具不依赖铁钉胶水，依靠榫卯结构咬合成型。工匠精准测算木料角度，凿榫眼、削榫头，凹凸相互契合，实现稳固衔接。每一处拼接无需辅材，顺应木材肌理，历经岁月依旧结实耐用。从选料开料、造型雕琢，到反复打磨、精细抛光，整套工序恪守古法。榫卯不止是工艺技巧，更是古人天人合一的造物智慧，将力学原理融入木器之中。方寸构件环环相扣，刚柔相生，让红木家具兼具实用价值与东方美学，承载绵延千年的中式匠心。

desc: China, as one of the world’s oldest civilizations, seeded countless traditions, technologies, and customs that spread across Korea and Japan. From the Four Great Inventions to language, clothing, and foodways, much of what’s now branded as Japanese 🇯🇵 Korean 🇰🇷 has roots in Chinese history. So why do so few people know this? Over time, borrowed traditions were localized and rebranded, while modern politics and national pride made it easier to emphasize difference rather than shared origins. This isn’t about shaming other nations or cultures though. It’s about recognizing that much of East Asia’s heritage is interconnected, and that ignoring China’s role distorts the region’s shared history. • • • #asia #chinaa #japan #korea #cultures

desc: The Wa People: From the Awa Mountains to the Modern World  The Wa are one of China’s most ancient and distinctive ethnic groups. They live primarily in the Awa Mountain region of southwestern Yunnan Province, especially in Cangyuan and Ximeng. For generations, they have lived among the rugged mountains and are often known as the “children of the Awa Mountains.”  Because many Wa communities were historically located in remote mountainous areas, some regions preserved social structures and cultural traditions with very ancient roots well into the twentieth century. During ethnographic surveys conducted in the early years of the People’s Republic of China, scholars summarized the Wa people’s remarkable historical transformation with a widely quoted phrase:  “Transitioning directly from the late stage of primitive society to socialist society.”  This phrase does not suggest that the Wa people lived in a “Stone Age” condition. Rather, it refers to the fact that some Wa communities did not pass through the full historical sequence of slave, feudal, and capitalist societies. Instead, under the impetus of modern state-building and profound social transformation, they entered modern society within a relatively short historical period.  Over the centuries, the Wa people have created a rich and distinctive cultural heritage, including the Wooden Drum tradition, the epic Sigangli, the famous Hair-Swing Dance, traditional folk songs, and a wealth of oral history passed down through generations. Today, the Awa Mountains remain a place where vibrant ethnic traditions coexist with modern development.  From remote mountain villages to participation in the modern globalized world, the story of the Wa people represents one of the most remarkable examples of social transformation in China’s ethnic history.  #🇨🇳 #Chinese #WaPeople #Ethnic #Minority

desc: After spending 10 days in China, one thing became very clear to me. The conversation shouldn’t be “China vs India.” China is competing on a different playing field altogether. desc: Somehow we’ve become so used to delayed trains, broken infrastructure, cash payments, paperwork, and inefficient public services that when a country gets these basics right, we call it “the future.” The future isn’t digital payments or high-speed rail. It’s the present.  While China is getting all those things right and more, we are stuck with fighting each other over petty topics.  That’s what the present is supposed to look like - clean cities, efficient public transport, systems are work for the people.  After travelling through China, I realised that what people call “living in 2050” is just the result of decades of investment in infrastructure and public services. Whether you agree with China’s political system or not, it’s hard not to notice what can happen when development becomes a national priority. Maybe China isn’t ahead of everyone else. Maybe the rest of us have just accepted less than we should. #china #china2050 #chinatravel #travelinchina #solotraveller

So if you want to take cool pictures at night, it is important that you try to do everything before 22.00, since that is when most cities turn off their lights.  I further also share some additional insights on the next slides and I am also happy to make a part 2 to discuss any other things you may find helpful to know. desc: 🍜 Best Foods to Try in China (For Foreigners) 🇨🇳 	1.	Dumplings (饺子, Jiǎozi) – Classic Chinese dish with meat or veggies inside. 	2.	Hotpot (火锅, Huǒguō) – Cook your own meat & vegetables in spicy or mild soup. 	3.	Peking Duck (北京烤鸭, Běijīng kǎoyā) – Crispy roast duck, famous in Beijing. 	4.	Fried Rice (炒饭, Chǎofàn) – Simple but flavorful, with egg, meat, or seafood. 	5.	Kung Pao Chicken (宫保鸡丁, Gōngbǎo jīdīng) – Spicy chicken with peanuts and peppers. 	6.	Sweet & Sour Pork (糖醋里脊, Táng cù lǐjǐ) – Sweet, tangy, and crunchy. 	7.	Baozi (包子) – Steamed buns filled with pork, beef, or veggies. 	8.	Noodles (面条, Miàntiáo) – Try Lanzhou hand-pulled noodles or Chongqing spicy noodles. 	9.	Spring Rolls (春卷, Chūnjuǎn) – Crispy rolls filled with vegetables/meat. 	10.	Mapo Tofu (麻婆豆腐, Mápó dòufu) – Spicy tofu with minced meat, famous in Sichuan. #chinatiktok #fyp #viral #china #food

desc: The Secret in the Blood: Why This Chinese Toddler Sparked a DNA Mystery In the bustling city of Yancheng, Jiangsu Province, life for one young couple seemed perfectly ordinary—until their daughter, Guojiang, began to transform before their very eyes. When Guojiang was born in May 2022, she looked like any other local infant. But nature had a hidden script waiting to be read. Around her eight-month milestone, the deep brown eyes her parents expected began to clear into a piercing, crystalline blue. By her first birthday, her dark hair didn’t just grow; it spiraled into golden, honey-blonde curls. The Shadow of Doubt Confusion quickly turned to anxiety. In a community where such features were unheard of, the couple faced a harrowing question: Was there a mistake at the hospital? The fear of a “switched baby” led them to the only place that could provide the truth—a genetic laboratory. A Genetic Ghost Returns The DNA results came back with 100% certainty: Guojiang was their biological child. Relieved but still baffled, the family began a deep dive into their genealogy. The answer lay buried four generations deep. It turned out the father’s great-great-grandfather was a Russian man who had settled in China decades ago, marrying a local woman from Henan. How It Happened Genetics often behave like a game of hide-and-seek. Traits for blue eyes and blonde hair are typically recessive. For them to appear, a child must inherit the specific gene from both parents. • The Sleeper Gene: For over a century, this Russian genetic marker traveled silently through the family line, masked by dominant Chinese traits. • The Perfect Match: By a statistical miracle, both parents carried a fragment of this hidden ancestry, and those fragments finally met in Guojiang. Today, Guojiang is a local celebrity—a living bridge between two cultures and a stunning reminder that our ancestors never truly leave us; they just wait for the right moment to reappear. #Genetics #FamilyMystery #DNAtest #ModernMiracle #Ancestry ScienceExplained ViralStory Identity HeritageDiscovery GuojiangStory

desc: China can be amazing, but there are things nobody prepares you for. You can live here for years, study, work and build a life here — but your foreign passport can still make simple things complicated. Some hotels won’t accept foreigners, some landlords don’t want foreign tenants, and the cameras are EVERYWHERE. As a student, your university can have strict rules around travel and activities. And WeChat? There are certain things you simply cannot freely post or discuss. Then there are the everyday experiences: booking a taxi and having the driver cancel after seeing you’re foreign, people staring, taking pictures without permission, touching your hair, or treating you differently because you’re Black. China has given me beautiful experiences, but also uncomfortable ones. These are the things I wish someone told me before moving here. 🇨🇳🤍 #ChinaLife #LivingInChina  #StudyInChina #lifeinchina

desc: 56 ethnic groups in China. China is a multi-ethnic country with 56 ethnic groups. Each ethnic group has its own unique culture, language, traditions, and customs. The Han nationality is the largest ethnic group in China, accounting for the vast majority of the population. They have a long history and rich cultural heritage, including traditional literature, art, architecture, and cuisine. Among the other 55 ethnic minorities, there are many with distinctive characteristics. For example, the Zhuang ethnic group is known for its beautiful folk songs and colorful brocade. The Miao ethnic group is famous for its exquisite silver ornaments and unique embroidery. The Yi ethnic group has a profound traditional culture and lively folk dances. The Tibetan ethnic group lives mainly in Tibet Autonomous Region and some other areas. They have a unique religious culture and magnificent architecture such as Potala Palace. The Uygur ethnic group in Xinjiang has a rich musical and dance culture, and their traditional handicrafts like carpets and silk fabrics are highly regarded. The ethnic minorities also have their own languages. Some ethnic groups have their own written languages, while others pass on their cultures through oral traditions. Each ethnic group's festivals are also diverse and colorful. For instance, the Dai ethnic group's Water Splashing Festival is full of joy and vitality. In China, all ethnic groups live in harmony and jointly create a beautiful homeland. The Chinese government has been committed to protecting the rights and interests of ethnic minorities and promoting the development and prosperity of ethnic cultures.China culture, China travel,#chinatravel #china #chinatiktok #travel

desc: Watching this series—of which this video is Part 2—you might come away thinking there are a LOT of things that bother me about living in China. But honestly, that couldn’t be further from the truth. Overall, I absolutely love living here. Most of the things we talk about are simply cultural differences or minor frustrations that, after 16 years in China, I barely even notice in everyday life anymore. My experience here as a foreigner has been overwhelmingly positive, and a huge part of that comes down to the people. The vast majority of Chinese people I’ve met over the years have been incredibly kind, friendly and welcoming—and that’s one of the biggest reasons China has felt like home for so long. But I also think that genuinely loving a place means being able to talk honestly about it. I don’t want my videos to present China as either the perfect country some people imagine it to be, or the terrible place others insist it is. Neither reflects the China I’ve actually experienced. Like anywhere else, there are things I love, things I don’t understand, things that frustrate me, and occasionally things I genuinely believe could and should improve. So this series isn’t about complaining about China. It’s about sharing a more complete picture of what living here for 16 years has actually been like—the good, the bad, the funny, the frustrating and everything in between. Some of these things are simply cultural differences that I’ve learned to accept. Others are things I genuinely think are worth talking about. And for those of you watching from outside China, perhaps some of them will also give you a better idea of what to expect if you ever come here yourself. After 16 years, China is home to me. And I think being honest about your home—including its imperfections—is far more meaningful than pretending everything about it is perfect.

desc: China never fails to amaze me😮‍💨 #luxchongzuo #chongqing #china #travel #fyp

China is one of the most regionally diverse cultures on earth. Hundreds of dialects, distinct customs, and value systems that shift province by province. And over centuries, each region developed its own reputation, its own strengths, its own identity that got passed down through generations. The Hakka were the nomads of China. Less than 10% of the population and yet they produced Sun Yat-sen, Deng Xiaoping, Lee Kuan Yew, and Tsai Ing-wen. In almost every country they settled in, they rose to the top of political power. The Cantonese were the first to leave, the first to absorb the West, and operating from a Hong Kong with creative freedoms the mainland never had, they became the tastemakers. Bruce Lee. Wong Kar-wai. Leslie Cheung. Anita Mui. They didn’t just participate in culture. They set the standard for what Chinese culture looked and sounded like for the entire world. The Hokkien built the merchant backbone of Southeast Asia before anyone was paying attention. And then they kept going. Robert Kuok. Henry Sy. Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia and the entire infrastructure of the AI revolution, born in Tainan, one of the oldest Hokkien cities in the world. Century after century, industry after industry. And Jiangnan, covering Shanghai, Zhejiang, and Jiangsu, produced the scholars. Confucian exam culture ran deepest here. That tradition didn’t disappear, it just modernized into Jack Ma, Jerry Yang, and some of the most influential tech founders of the last thirty years. These aren’t stereotypes. They’re patterns. Built over centuries of geography, migration, trade, and survival, and passed down through every generation that followed. This is why Chinese people still ask where you’re from. Your region carries a story. Your family carried it forward. Which one are you? Drop it in the comments 👇  #china #chinese #hongkong #hakka #cantonese

What shocked many even more was that the boy had reportedly performed better before the intense tutoring began. The story quickly spread across Weibo, where many questioned the immense academic pressure placed on children. Some argued that endless studying without enough rest may have led to stress and burnout, affecting the boy's ability to perform.

desc: Chilled air, busy days,we stride ahead, gathering every glow and warmth for winter. making delicious traditional bamboo rat dishes. rural life in China countryside life and cooking Chinese craftswomen daily life vlog Chinese culture Chinese heritage Chinese food Chinese village Chinese craft Chinese lifestyle explore China. Bamboo rat farming emerged in China as a notable and profitable niche within the specialty livestock sector. Primarily concentrated in the southern and southwestern provinces like Guangxi, Guangdong, and Yunnan, these large rodents are valued for their low-maintenance husbandry, efficient feed conversion, and high market demand. Farmers raise them in purpose-built, multi-tiered concrete pens, feeding them primarily a diet of bamboo, grass, and some supplemental grains. The animals are prized for their lean, tender meat, which is considered a delicacy and believed in traditional Chinese medicine to have warming properties. While the industry faced a significant setback following a nationwide wildlife trade ban in 2020 due to pandemic concerns, it continues in a more regulated form, representing a unique intersection of rural entrepreneurship, traditional culinary tastes, and ongoing debates about sustainable and safe animal agriculture in modern China. In Chinese cuisine, the bamboo rat is transformed from a farmed rodent into a celebrated delicacy, often referred to as "bamboo mouse" or "zhu shu" (竹鼠). Its meat is prized for a fine texture and a mild, clean flavor, subtly sweet and often compared to rabbit or dark-meat chicken. The most traditional and revered preparation is "Stewed Bamboo Rat with Chinese Herbs" (药膳竹鼠), a hearty, nourishing clay-pot dish where the meat is braised for hours with goji berries, jujubes, astragalus, and ginger, believed to replenish energy and warmth in the body. However, it is also boldly seasoned in regional specialties; in Guangxi, it might be dry-fried with chili and Sichuan peppercorns for a fragrant, numbing spice, or in Guangdong, roasted until the skin is crackling and golden. Once a staple of rural banquets and a symbol of hospitality in southern regions, consumption of bamboo rat dishes has become more subdued and controversial since the wildlife trade ban, but it remains a potent symbol of a distinct regional food culture that values utilizing unique local resources. #fyp #foryou #foryoupage #fypシ #fypシ゚viral @LiXiaoAi @LiXiaoAi

desc: A true story from Oklahoma, USA: A Chinese woman converted to Islam, but her husband refused. God blessed them with a son and a daughter. However, the husband divorced his wife, took the children with him to America, and forbade the mother from seeing them or travelling to them. The mother remained in China, patient, steadfast, and unwavering in her faith, even if the price was the loss of her husband and children forever. Many years passed… Then suddenly, after more than 15 years, her eldest daughter (now in her twenties) called her and said, "Mom, please come visit us in Oklahoma. Dad has finally agreed." The mother travelled immediately. As soon as she arrived at the Oklahoma airport, she took out her phone, searched for the nearest Islamiccentree or mosque to her daughter's address, wrote the number and address on a piece of paper, gave it to her daughter, and said, "If anything happens to me, call this number immediately." The daughter asked in surprise, "Who are they?"  “They are my brothers,” the mother said calmly and confidently. The daughter didn’t pay much attention to the matter. The mother was Chinese, knew no one in America, and didn’t know the mosque, who ran it, or the nationalities of its worshippers… but as a Muslim, she knew that the words “brother” and “sister” in Islam weren’t just words, but a reality. Just three days after her arrival… the mother, may God have mercy on her, passed away suddenly, without any prior illness. The daughter immediately remembered her mother’s words and called the number her mother had given her. What happened next was astonishing: it turned out that the mosque the mother had randomly chosen from the internet was a small mosque in the suburbs of Oklahoma, which owned a plot of land the community had purchased years earlier to be an Islamic cemetery… but they had spent five whole years fighting in the courts to obtain a burial permit, and hadn’t been allowed to bury any Muslims there during that entire time. Just now—only a few days before the Chinese sister’s death—official approval was finally granted, and they could legally use the cemetery.  The call came from the daughter, the very next day after the permit was issued! The imam of the mosque himself went to meet the family and told the daughter, "The first grave to be dug in this new cemetery will be your mother's, as an honour to her and to us." On Friday, the mosque was overflowing with people they had never seen before, and an incredible, majestic funeral procession took place: hundreds of people walked behind the coffin, men and women of every race—white, black, Arab, Indian, African, Asian… A sight that the daughter, her brother, and even their father had never witnessed before.  The family was shocked and wept, asking, "Who are these people?! What is their relationship to our mother?" The imam replied that they were her brothers in Islam. In Islam, a Muslim is the brother of another Muslim. After the burial, the daughter took out a small piece of paper she found in her mother's bag. It was written in Arabic in her mother's handwriting. She asked the sheikh to tell them what was written on it. He said, "She wrote: 'O God, guide my children… O God, guide my sons…'" When the sheikh translated the supplication for them, her ex-husband said, "I want the grave next to hers." The sheikh told him, "The price for that is for you to bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God." He recited the two testimonies of faith and embraced Islam. That same night, her son also embraced Islam and recited the two testimonies of faith. We ask God to forgive her, have mercy on her, and grant her a spacious place in Paradise. This story is 100% true and witnessed by all the Muslims in the area. It has been previously recounted on religious programs. ✍️ Ali Abdul  Al-Raziq

Xi'an · The Ancient Capital Don't Miss: Terracotta Army, City Wall, Giant Wild Goose Pagoda Eat: Hand-pulled Noodles in Spicy Sauce, Chinese Hamburger (Rou Jia Mo) 	 4. Chongqing · The Cyberpunk Mountain City Don't Miss: Hongya Cave, Liziba Monorail, Yangtze River Cableway Eat: Spicy Hot Pot 	 5. Chengdu · Pandas & Slow Living Don't Miss: Giant Panda Breeding Base, Jinli Ancient Street, Wuhou Shrine Eat: Sichuan Hotpot, Dan Dan Noodles, Mapo Tofu 	 6. Guangzhou · The Food Capital Don't Miss: Canton Tower, Chen Clan Academy, Yongqing Fang Eat: Dim Sum, Claypot Rice, Roast Goose, Double-Skin Milk 	 7. Harbin · The Ice Kingdom Don't Miss: Ice and Snow World, St. Sophia Cathedral Best Time: December – February ❄️ 	 8. Yunnan · The Land of Eternal Spring Don't Miss: Erhai Lake (Dali), Old Town of Lijiang, Tiger Leaping Gorge, Stone Forest Eat: Across-the-Bridge Noodles, Steam Pot Chicken, Grilled Milk Fan 	 9. Hangzhou · Heaven on Earth Don't Miss: West Lake, Lingyin Temple, Longjing Tea Village Eat: Dongpo Pork, Longjing Shrimp 	 10. Zhangjiajie · Avatar Mountains Don't Miss: Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, Tianmen Mountain, Glass Skywalk Eat: Tujia Three-Pot Stew, Sour and Spicy Fish 	 ⚠️ Avoid China’s public holidays (especially Labor Day in May, National Day in October, and Spring Festival). desc: For decades, they lived simply. The two of them shared a single meal that cost just 18 yuan—about $2.50—and that was enough. Du Yingrong was a teacher. His wife, Lu Suying, was a physician. They worked at the same college in Shanghai, built a quiet life together, and chose not to have children. Those who knew them often said they never seemed to desire luxury. They lived modestly and spent very little on themselves. Then, in early 2018, everything changed. While walking past Shanghai Yoda Cardiothoracic Hospital, Du noticed a poster asking for help. It told the stories of children born with heart defects whose families couldn't afford life-saving surgery. He returned home and spoke with Lu. Together, they decided to donate 500,000 yuan—enough to fund heart operations for ten children. But they didn't stop there. Over the following years, they quietly donated a total of 5 million yuan—around $735,000—helping pay for surgeries that saved the lives of 455 children. They never sought attention. In fact, almost no one knew what they had done. Du died in 2018 at the age of 81. Lu passed away last year at 92. Their extraordinary generosity remained a secret until a charity exhibition held in their honor in Shanghai a few weeks ago, where many people heard their names for the very first time. They changed the lives of 455 children—not for praise, not for fame, but simply because they believed it was the right thing to do. #kindness  #kindnessisfree  #love

desc: 5 reasons China is so different from the U.S., explained through cultural theory from Trompenaars, Schwartz, and Hofstede. China and the United States are running on opposite cultural operating systems. The same situation reads as harmony in one and chaos in the other. First, Trompenaars communitarianism. China thinks group first. Citizens and the government weigh how decisions affect everyone else, which produces stability. Americans think self first, which produces friction. Second, Schwartz's benevolence. China prioritizes loyalty and care for the community. America prioritizes personal achievement. Third, Schwartz's security dimension. Chinese culture treats social order and stability as the goal. American culture treats liberty as the goal, even when that liberty produces instability. Fourth, Hofstede's long-term orientation. China plans in decades and accepts small sacrifices now for larger gains in twenty years. The United States plans in quarters and election cycles, taking small wins today and trading the future for them. Fifth, Hofstede's quality of life dimension. The Chinese measure success in time with family, friends, and hobbies. Americans measure success in income and possessions. Neither system is better or worse. They are different. The mistake is judging Chinese behavior by American values, then calling the result a failure. The Chinese are not failing at being American. They are succeeding at being Chinese. Full breakdown is on Substack today at culturalperspective.com for paid subscribers. #CulturalPerspective #China #ChineseCulture #CulturalTheory #USChina

desc: A Chinese father feeding his daughter dumplings before her wedding went viral because of one small gesture that said everything about a lifetime of love. In Shanxi Province in northern China, there is a tradition known as the Last Bite. Before a bride leaves her family home on her wedding day, dressed in traditional red, her father feeds her one final meal. It is not a grand ceremony. There are no speeches or formal rituals surrounding it. It is simply a father and his daughter sitting together, sharing food, for the last time before everything changes. A video of one such moment went viral on Reddit in May 2026, drawing millions of views and an outpouring of emotion from people across the world who had never heard of the tradition before watching it. In the clip, the bride sits across from her father in her red wedding attire. He prepares a dumpling and lifts it toward her mouth. Then he pauses, pulls it back slightly, and blows on it to cool it down before offering it to her again. The bride's smile crumbled. Her father's composure went with it. Both began to cry before either of them could stop it. The bride took the bowl and chopsticks from him, trying to compose herself. Her father stood, walked to another part of the room, and sat alone to wipe his eyes. The tradition itself carries a significance that goes beyond the meal. In Chinese culture, particularly in Shanxi, feeding a child is one of the most fundamental expressions of parental love and responsibility. The act of a father feeding his daughter represents everything he has provided for her since birth, care, protection, nourishment, and presence. The Last Bite is the formal acknowledgment that this chapter is ending. It does not mean he will never feed her again, or that their relationship ends at the wedding door. It means she is no longer a child in her father's home. She is stepping into a new life, and he is sending her there the same way he has always cared for her, by making sure her food is not too hot. China is an extraordinarily diverse country with over 50 distinct ethnic groups and centuries of regional traditions that vary significantly from province to province. The Last Bite is specific to certain communities in Shanxi and is not a universal Chinese custom. But the emotion it captures is universal in every sense. Every parent who has ever blown on food to cool it for a child, every child who has ever been on the receiving end of that gesture without thinking twice about it, understands what that moment in the video means. The gesture is so small and so ordinary that it barely registers in daily life. At a wedding, with everything it represents, it becomes almost unbearable. #LastBite #ChineseWeddingTradition #Heartwarming

desc: Quite a few of you said you wanted to see my take on dating culture differences between China and the U.S. or between the east and the west so here it is ❤️  We’ve seen how in C-dramas it can take 23 episodes before the couple finally holds hands or kiss… meanwhile in American movies it’s a complete different pace. And that difference reflects a lot of real-life dating culture 🤭 Looking back on my own dating experiences in the U.S. as a Chinese woman from China, there were definitely so many moments of confusion and cultural misunderstanding haha. I still remember a guy texting me after our first date saying he was disappointed there wasn’t a first-date kiss because he felt like he had somehow “failed” me meanwhile I was just sitting there extremely confused lol.  I think the world is so big, but also very small at the same time 🌍 You may totally find your soulmate who maybe from another culture! There’s no “right” way to date, just different cultural expectations, communication styles, and ways people express interest. So I hope this post helps people from both Eastern and Western cultures understand each other a little better and maybe even helps some future couples navigate dating more smoothly ✨ Let me know if I missed anything, if your experiences were different, or if you have any funny cross-cultural dating stories 👀 And let me know what other East vs. West topics you want to see next 🫶 #dating #datingculture #eastvswest #immigrant #chinese

desc: Have you ever noticed this simple difference? Westerners speak in “I”, while Chinese people naturally speak in “we.” It’s not an accident — it’s a window into two completely different cultural operating systems. In the West, identity is individual. In China, identity is collective — shaped by groups, circles, and networks that run deeper than most outsiders ever imagine. For thousands of years, Chinese people weren’t united by the nation-state. They were united by hometown circles, school circles, industry circles — what we call quanzi. Even today, business, trust, and cooperation still run through these invisible networks. Most foreigners fail in China not because of business knowledge, but because they never understand how these circles work — or how group-first values shape decisions and relationships. If you want to connect deeply with China, start by understanding circles (quanzi), not just “culture.” Tomorrow (Nov 30), I’m doing a 90-minute session Understanding Chinese Culture. Things I wish I knew before going to China China is a fascinating place, but it can be overwhelming if you're not prepared! Here are some essential tips to make your trip smoother:  1. Download Amap for navigation since Google Maps won't help you here.  2. High-speed trains are often better than flying for city-to-city travel.  3. Cash is becoming obsolete; use Alipay or WeChat Pay for convenience.  4. Be cautious with power banks at airports; they can be confiscated if not marked properly.  5. Avoid using foreign cards for payments over 200 RMB to dodge extra fees.  6. Don't rely solely on translation apps; screenshotting menus works better.  7. Explore local markets and neighborhoods for the best experiences!  China is easier than it seems once you have the basics sorted. desc: While dumplings are famous, China’s baozi (steamed buns) are just as delicious and diverse! Here are 6 regional favorites: 	 1. Xinjiang Baked Baozi (Samsa) Thin dough wrapped around spiced lamb, onions, and cumin—crispy outside, juicy inside. 	 2. Jiangsu Crab Roe Soup Bun Invented centuries ago, these delicate buns are filled with crab meat and rich broth. The skin is so thin it almost melts! 	 3. Shanghai Pan-Fried Buns (Shengjianbao) Crispy bottom, soft top, and filled with savory pork and hot, flavorful soup. A perfect bite! 	 4. Hangzhou Xiaolongbao Thin, translucent wrappers hold generous filling and steaming broth—often enjoyed with a straw for the soup first! 	 5. Guangdong Char Siu Bao A Cantonese dim sum classic! Fluffy buns stuffed with sweet-and-savory barbecued pork. 	 6. Shandong Steam-Fried Buns Golden-crisp at the bottom, soft on top, with rich fillings. Masterfully cooked with water-based pan-frying for the perfect texture. 	 Which one would you try first? 🥢 #chinesefood #china #baozi #ChineseCulture #tourguide

desc: 👋 Hey, language learners! Did you know that in Chinese, there’s a specific word for every single family member? It's not just "uncle" or "aunt" like in English. It's WAY more detailed! 👉 For example: Your dad’s older brother? He’s 伯伯 (bóbo). Dad’s younger brother? He’s 叔叔 (shūshu). Mom’s brother? That’s 舅舅 (jiùjiu). And it doesn’t stop there! Even your cousins have different titles based on their gender and whether they’re older or younger than you. 🗣️ Why does this matter? Because if you use the wrong title, it might sound a bit odd—or even rude! 😅 ✨ Learning these terms shows respect and understanding of Chinese culture. So, if you want to impress your Chinese friends or family, master those family words! 💬 Let me know in the comments: Did you know about this? Which family word do you find the most interesting? 🤔 #LearnChinese #FamilyTitles #LanguageTips

desc: Let me get this straight - travelling China changed the way I view life forever. Feel free to ask me any questions. It was like entering a new planet, a planet where my health and well-being was considered as a priority, a necessity, as rather than something to be made money off of. Walking around the cities, speaking to people, workers, locals, interacting with supermarkets, advertisements - I’m not trying to be tricked. Something I never quite stressed enough about my experience - feeling safe as a female solo traveller, wandering the streets at night, doing activities alone, rather than having to check myself constantly - something you will find woman does subconsciously every day - finally not having to watch myself from an outsider’s viewpoint, imagine how I look.  Something capitalist societies thrive off of - women constantly watching themselves, not being present, wondering what could be the next thing they change about themselves that makes them finally feel enough - this all forbidding them from fully EXPERIENCING. Imagine coming to China and being given the permission to finally experience life through your own eyes, not the eyes of the people on the streets, and that being…. NORMALISED. Finally being able to face yourself, be present, be present, be present, what a gift that some of us have not fully been immersed in yet. #china #traveltips #capitalism #sleepertrains #beijingwinterolympics

desc: A Chinese father feeding his daughter dumplings before her wedding went viral because of one small gesture that said everything about a lifetime of love. In Shanxi Province in northern China, there is a tradition known as the Last Bite. Before a bride leaves her family home on her wedding day, dressed in traditional red, her father feeds her one final meal. It is not a grand ceremony. There are no speeches or formal rituals surrounding it. It is simply a father and his daughter sitting together, sharing food, for the last time before everything changes. A video of one such moment went viral on Reddit in May 2026, drawing millions of views and an outpouring of emotion from people across the world who had never heard of the tradition before watching it. In the clip, the bride sits across from her father in her red wedding attire. He prepares a dumpling and lifts it toward her mouth. Then he pauses, pulls it back slightly, and blows on it to cool it down before offering it to her again. The bride's smile crumbled. Her father's composure went with it. Both began to cry before either of them could stop it. The bride took the bowl and chopsticks from him, trying to compose herself. Her father stood, walked to another part of the room, and sat alone to wipe his eyes. The tradition itself carries a significance that goes beyond the meal. In Chinese culture, particularly in Shanxi, feeding a child is one of the most fundamental expressions of parental love and responsibility. The act of a father feeding his daughter represents everything he has provided for her since birth, care, protection, nourishment, and presence. The Last Bite is the formal acknowledgment that this chapter is ending. It does not mean he will never feed her again, or that their relationship ends at the wedding door. It means she is no longer a child in her father's home. She is stepping into a new life, and he is sending her there the same way he has always cared for her, by making sure her food is not too hot. China is an extraordinarily diverse country with over 50 distinct ethnic groups and centuries of regional traditions that vary significantly from province to province. The Last Bite is specific to certain communities in Shanxi and is not a universal Chinese custom. But the emotion it captures is universal in every sense. Every parent who has ever blown on food to cool it for a child, every child who has ever been on the receiving end of that gesture without thinking twice about it, understands what that moment in the video means. The gesture is so small and so ordinary that it barely registers in daily life. At a wedding, with everything it represents, it becomes almost unbearable. #LastBite #ChineseWeddingTradition #heartwarming

I love the life our family has built here in China—the rhythm of our days, the opportunities, the community. But beneath that gratitude, there’s a question that keeps surfacing: Is this really the right place for our children?

A Quiet Life, an Extraordinary Legacy 📷 Du Yingrong and Lu Suying lived a remarkably simple life in China. The childless couple carefully saved money and were known for sharing inexpensive meals costing only a few dollars. But behind their modest lifestyle was an extraordinary act of kindness. After learning about children suffering from congenital heart disease, the couple donated 5 million yuan—around $735,000—to help fund lifesaving treatment. Their generosity eventually helped 455 children receive the medical care they desperately needed. They never lived extravagantly or sought attention for what they had done. Instead, they chose to use their savings to give vulnerable children a healthier future. Their beautiful story proves that true wealth isn’t measured by what we keep, but by how many lives we touch. 📷 See less
